A contract arrives.
  
A dispute emerges.
  
A regulatory issue appears.
  
A business team asks for urgent advice.
  
Legal responds.
  
Then the next issue arrives.
  
This model may keep the department busy—but it does not necessarily make it strategic.
  
Legal transformation requires a different approach.
  
It begins with asking:
  
Why are we doing this manually?
  
Why does the same issue keep recurring?
  
Can we standardise it?
  
Can we automate it?
  
Can we move legal review earlier in the process?
  
Can data help us identify trends?
  
Can the business access appropriate guidance without waiting for Legal every time?
  
Transformation can involve:
  
• Legal technology

 • Standardisation
 • Playbooks
 • Knowledge management
 • Matter management
 • Data and analytics
 • Workflow automation
 • AI-assisted legal processes
 • External counsel optimisation
 • Risk dashboards
 • Legal performance metrics
  
But technology alone does not transform a legal department.
  
Leadership does.
  
The objective should be to redesign the legal function around the needs of the business.
  
Routine work should become more efficient.
  
High-risk matters should receive greater attention.
  
Business teams should receive clearer guidance.
  
Senior lawyers should spend more time on strategic matters.
  
Management should gain better visibility into legal risk and performance.
  
And the legal function should increasingly operate as a source of business intelligence, not merely legal advice.

Legal transformation is therefore not a technology project.

The vendor delivers more value, yet risks a smaller contract. That is the SaaS Pricing Paradox, when you price only on human logins, customer efficiency can become revenue erosion.

Three realities make the transition difficult:

* Outcomes are harder to bill than seats.
Pay per resolved ticket sounds simple. Until the customer reopens it three days later.

Who pays when an AI qualified lead never converts? Without clear definitions, attribution rules, and dispute mechanisms, outcome pricing becomes an argument over what done means.

* Intelligence has a compute floor.
Agentic workflows consume inference, retrieval, and integration resources with every task. Multi step reasoning and repeated retries can make apparently valuable activity unprofitable.

If pricing ignores delivery costs, your busiest customer could become your least profitable one. Usage growth is not automatically margin growth.

* A hybrid model offers a practical path.
A base platform fee can cover governance, security, data management, and administrative access, creating a predictable revenue floor.

Work unit metering can charge for discrete, verifiable work,  a validated claim, a reconciled transaction, or a resolved ticket under agreed rules.

The key is defining the billable unit clearly, pricing for delivery costs, and giving customers visibility into spend. Not every product needs to abandon seats, but seats alone may no longer reflect the value delivered.

Software is no longer just a canvas for human work. It is increasingly doing the work itself.

If your product helps customers grow without hiring, your business model must grow without depending on their headcount. Counting chairs is no longer enough.

How is your board addressing seat-count compression at renewal: defending seats, metering work, or redesigning the model.

Why?.. Clients are making more informed decisions around their strategic hires. They’re taking more time to define what they actually need, where the role sits within the wider business and what success looks like. And some candidates are 'passively looking' but they’re often running multiple processes at once. It’s not unusual to see multiple offers on the table.
  
Counter-offers are back. We’re regularly seeing retention moves, title bumps and pay adjustments as employers work to hold onto their best people. Modernisation is still happening. Platform uplift, cloud, security, integration, data and reliability work continues, even when organisations are being more cautious around headcount.

Here are 10 mistakes that can genuinely hurt you (or your business) when using AI tools:
 
Feeding it sensitive data you can't take back — pasting client contracts, medical records, passwords, API keys, or proprietary business plans into a chat. Once it's in a prompt, assume it could be logged or seen by someone else.

Trusting facts without verification — AI can state wrong information confidently. Never publish, act on, or teach a fact (stats, laws, medical/legal claims, historical details) without checking it against a real source, especially for anything client-facing.

Letting it make financial or legal decisions unsupervised — using AI-generated numbers in a business plan, tax filing, or contract without a professional reviewing it. It's a drafting tool, not an accountant or lawyer.

Running AI-written code without reading it — especially anything that touches money, user data, deletes files, or sends messages. Unreviewed code can leak data or break production systems.

Publishing AI content as-is under your name — especially for coaching/education businesses like FISL, where trust is the product. Unedited AI text often reads generic, sometimes hallucinates, and can quietly damage credibility.

Automating actions without a human checkpoint — letting an automation (n8n, Zapier, agents) send emails, post content, or message clients with zero review step. One bad output can go out to hundreds of people before you notice.

Ignoring copyright and IP exposure — using AI to generate content "in the style of" a real brand, artist, or using copyrighted lyrics/text, then publishing it commercially. This can create real legal risk.

Over-trusting AI on other people's data — asking it to profile, diagnose, or make judgments about a specific real person (health, character, legal risk) as if it has authority it doesn't have.

Skipping security basics in AI-assisted builds — vibe-coding an app or automation without validating inputs, securing API keys, or thinking about who else could access the data flowing through it.

Using it as a substitute for real judgment on high-stakes calls — hiring decisions, firing someone, big financial commitments, or client disputes. AI can help you think it through, but the accountability and final call should stay human.

AI Does Not Need To Own Information To Reason About It.
What is the role of ZDR?

Many companies asks a question: 
What happens to my data after the AI answers?

When we give AI 
-> Source code, 
-> a legal contract.
-> A financial report.
-> Customer information.
-> Unreleased product design.
-> Internal research.

The AI needs to see this information to help. That is unavoidable.
But does the company operating that AI need to keep it afterward?
This is where Zero Data Retention or ZDR for short comes in.

What does it  mean?
Imagine hiring an extremely capable consultant.
You bring them into a secure room.
You place a confidential document on the table.
They read it, analyze it, answer your questions and help you solve the problem.

Then they leave and they don not:
-> photograph the document.
-> take a copy home.
-> add it to their personal archive.
-> use it later to train another employee.
The interaction happened.
The information was processed.
But it was not retained as content after the job finished.

That is roughly what Zero Data Retention is trying to achieve.
The AI still needs temporary access to the information (the secure room) while processing your request. But the provider should not turn every interaction into a permanent memory.

Why does this matter?
Because AI is slowly moving from:
"Help me write an email."
toward:
"Help me operate my company."

And these are two completely different security problems.
If AI is going to analyze production systems, engineering repositories, contracts, medical information, financial models, intellectual property or internal strategy, companies need stronger guarantees about where that information goes.

The system is designed around:
"We don't need to keep your information in the first place."

That changes what companies can safely consider putting through AI.
Opening the door to deeper use of AI for enterprises, I think this will become increasingly important. 

But there is a catch.
Zero Data Retention is not magic.
There can also be operational metadata, security information and other records that are treated differently from the actual prompt and response.
So Zero Data Retention should never be understood as:
-> Nothing exists anywhere.
But more like:
-> What data is processed, where is it processed, what is stored, by whom, and for how long?

The best AI is not the one that remembers everything.
The smartest thing it can do... is know when to forget.
At least until we can powerful local AI... ZDR will matter more and more as new age Gold is Data and Information you provide.

For two weeks, Sarah* had been telling Chatty-P** what she needed to do after close.

Before a few months ago, she had kept reminders in three places, one of which was her head. That location had the worst search function and refused to close at bedtime.

"After close: update the forecast assumptions." "Look at the contractor renewal versus a permanent hire." "Book time with my manager about career development."

On Monday, close was finished.

"Can you organize my after-close notes into a checklist?"

The answer arrived with seven tidy headings, from FORECAST & PLANNING all the way down to, at the very bottom: CAREER & DEVELOPMENT. Sarah collapsed the first heading. Then the next. By the time CAREER & DEVELOPMENT appeared, she had hidden most of the work standing between her and it.

"That looks awesome," Cartoon Beverly observed.

"It is. My days of endless sticky notes are over."

The formatting was considerably calmer than the situation.

The follow-up emails were already arriving. "Just following up." "Now that close is over, could you take a look?" Sarah had promised to get to those "after close," which had seemed like a reasonable date when she typed it. Now everyone else had reached "after close" too.

The contractor question caught RoBev's attention. A department lead wanted help deciding: extend a contract, or make the case for a permanent role?

"So you'd compare the contractor cost with the cost of hiring?" RoBev asked.

"Eventually. First I'd want to know what they're doing. Are they clearing a backlog, or keeping up with work that arrives every week? Because if we hire based on a backlog, what happens when they finish it?"

"When did they ask?"

"Second day of close."

Sarah opened the thread. There was a newer message: "We've extended another six months. Would still appreciate your thoughts for the next renewal."

She put her pen down.

"That might have been the right decision," she said. "But I wanted to check."

Nobody escalated. The department needed an answer and made a decision with what it had. You could look at the completed tasks and miss the analysis that never happened between them.

Turns out the Robot Tax charges interest. Work accumulates while Sarah is busy with close, and some decisions won't wait. Next month's close is already on the calendar.

"What would you like to do more of?" Cartoon Beverly asked.

"Adding value. Like the contractor question. I want to be in the conversation while there's still something to decide."

"Have you booked the meeting with your manager?"

"I'll book that once I'm caught up."

I wondered how long Sarah had been waiting for that conversation.

Auditor's notes: Entry 14, filed. Close: complete. Decisions made before analysis: 1. Career conversation: pending.

I asked a former community college chancellor what she'd do differently about technology if she had her presidency back.  

Her answer had nothing to do with technology.  

“I’d make sure with my cabinet that we aren’t chasing technology just to “keep up”. I’d want to #1 stay away from having technology contracts where nobody can explain why we have it. No more contracts that nobody understands."

That's the pattern I see most often now with AI. Not resistance but blind acceptance. One person in the room sounds confident, and everyone else goes quiet.  

The fix isn't hiring a technologist. It's getting enough shared literacy that the room can actually deliberate.  

When your cabinet discusses AI, is it a deliberation or a blind acceptance? I'm genuinely curious how other institutions are handling this.

Contract staffing is back and booming in a big way. The American Staffing Association's August 2026 Index Report shows that contract roles have increased by nearly 6% YoY. You may think that's because of the cost of direct hires or not being able to find certain skillsets, but that's not entirely the case.

Business Insider came out with an article which takes a deep dive into why companies are moving more towards contract hring models in the age of AI and how there's now a distrust in the candidates they're vetting. I have some thoughts...

We've been in the middle of a candidate driven market for years, and I don't foresee that changing in the near future. And a lot of companies know this. So, can understand why companies want candidates to prove they are who they say they are. 

I strongly believe that a lot of companies, and my clients, have SELF-created the lack of trust they're claiming to have in their potential candidates. AI-driven ATS systems have gotten completely out of control.

"Jason, this person must have used AI to format their resume. They must not be that good if they can't create their own resumes and get past our fortress that is our AI-driven ATS system. I don't care if they're one of only 4 matches out of 250 applicants." 

Sorry, had to dramatize to prove a point. If you create these AI filters that are filtering out an overwhelming majority of applicants based on keywords...,how do you expect candidates to get past that? You reap what you sow.

I can't think of one job that doesn't have a gray area. These AI systems have been trained to be way too granular. My solution? Tweak your internal AI system to be more inclusive on job titles, filter out industries (if you absolutely must) and then train your internal TA-team on how to read between the lines on a resume. 

Put human eyes on a resume for 10-15 seconds. Arm your TA team with 3 technical questions that your hiring managers need and if a candidate can't answer them, rule them out. 

AI has it's place in saving people time in the workplace. I'm all for that. But use it to be more inclusive and actually be a human being to decide if they're a fit. Think that would solve a LOT of problems.
